Introduction
GreenUp links Veolia’s growth to a leverage cap
The group measured the debt headroom below this cap, then assessed what it could purchase with it
The headroom finances these tuck-ins, and we have identified one in particular: the Chauny incinerator
1. GreenUp announces net envelopes, which do not cap acquisitions
1.1 The envelopes are net; leverage, not the envelope, limits acquisitions
1.2 GreenUp’s capital allocation is based on net balances after disposals
1.3 Asset rotation adds purchases and sales together: it is the gross figure
1.4 Net outflows since 2024 are not comparable to the growth envelope
1.5 Clean Earth has four figures, and leverage retains the effect on debt
1.6 The disposal programme offsets the majority of Clean Earth’s value, partly after 2027
1.7 Each figure refers to a file, a page and a date of access
1.8 What we could not establish
2. The leverage cap Veolia sets itself binds before the rating agencies' thresholds
2.1 Leverage exceeds the cap in September 2026 and leaves only thin headroom at the end of 2027
2.2 Veolia’s definition exactly matches its published ratios
2.3 As at 30 September 2026, no leverage ratio falls below the cap
2.4 To end 2026 at the announced level will require an exceptional fourth quarter
2.5 The repayment of a hybrid security increases Veolia’s leverage more than Moody’s adjusted debt figure
2.6 The rating agencies' thresholds leave more headroom than Veolia's cap at the end of 2027
2.7 Refinancing increases the cost of debt without limiting capacity
2.8 What we could not establish
3. Thin headroom at the end of 2027, driven by EBITDA and disposals rather than by net free cash flow
3.1 At the end of 2027, the headroom below the cap remains narrow and is primarily due to the timing of the disposals
3.2 Net free cash flow does not cover all dividends
3.3 From 30 September 2026 to the end of 2027, debt falls due to the fourth quarter and the disposals
3.4 Disposals are more significant in terms of their timing than their multiples
3.5 The timing of the disposals and growth in 2027 have the greatest impact on the headroom
3.5.1 One assumption at a time: five factors can wipe out the headroom
3.5.2 Out of the 1,000 simulated outcomes, the cap is breached in a significant minority of cases
3.6 Efficiency drives EBITDA growth and remains the most fragile assumption
3.7 What we could not establish
4. The hazardous waste booster buys its growth rather than generating it
4.1 The booster grows first through acquisitions, paid for at a price that only synergies offset
4.2 The volume target has been reduced in line with the scope of operations, and Veolia is already exceeding it
4.3 In value terms, organic growth slows and acquisitions take over
4.3.1 In 2024 and 2025, the business grew organically
4.3.2 In 2026, acquisitions account for most of the growth
4.3.3 Organic investment accounts for only a small proportion compared with acquisitions
4.4 From the seller’s perspective, Clean Earth’s EBITDA is lower than Veolia’s budget
4.4.1 The multiple published by Veolia is based on high synergies
4.4.2 Enviri’s financial statements show lower EBITDA and slow growth
4.4.3 The first few months’ consolidated results are consistent with the budget, though this does not prove it
4.5 Clean Earth’s multiple ranges from 9 to 19 times, depending on the EBITDA figure used
4.6 Clean Harbors, the only direct comparable, commands prices on a par with Veolia’s
4.6.1 Clean Harbors combines a high headroom with low leverage
4.6.2 Before synergies, Clean Earth is valued on a par with its US peers
4.6.3 The other companies are not comparable or have yet to be valued
4.7 Peer group analysis validates the model’s central assumptions, but not its lower bound for Clean Earth
4.8 What we could not establish
5. The environmental liabilities associated with an acquisition determine the cost of due diligence, not the acquisition capacity
5.1 Assumed liabilities run into tens of millions and are excluded from net financial debt
5.2 Veolia’s closure provisions remain stable, except for the half-year period relating to Clean Earth
5.2.1 A balance dominated by site remediation
5.2.2 An increase in the first half of 2026 which Veolia does not attribute to
5.3 Clean Earth was recognised in the accounts before its liabilities were measured at fair value
5.3.1 A known purchase price, but liabilities that are still provisional
5.3.2 What the allocation of the purchase price will change
5.3.3 Authorised sites and financial guarantees to be monitored
5.4 Peer companies provide an order of magnitude, not a precise measure of Clean Earth’s liabilities
5.4.1 Clean Harbors has liabilities comparable to those of Veolia
5.4.2 Enviri provides an upper limit, without discounting
5.5 Off-balance-sheet exposure relates to litigation, PFAS and insurance limits
5.5.1 Veolia and the rating agencies identify the risk
5.5.2 Penalties at sites, a past that may resurface
5.5.3 PFAS represent a market for Veolia and a potential liability for a treatment centre
5.5.4 Insurance does not cover everything
5.6 The taxonomy classifies a portion of hazardous waste capex as ‘green’, without taking liabilities into account
5.7 GreenUp’s ESG indicators show little change following an acquisition in the hazardous waste sector
5.8 Provisions remain excluded from Veolia’s leverage ratio, and Moody’s does not include them in any line item
5.9 What we could not establish
6. If Séché has to sell an incinerator to acquire Flamme, Chauny is the tuck-in that Veolia could target
6.1 The 2027 headroom finances tuck-ins and no platforms
6.2 Veolia’s tuck-ins have names, a price and three published criteria
6.3 Séché is acquiring Flamme, and the Competition Authority is reviewing the transaction
6.4 If a disposal is required, the Chauny incinerator is the most easily separable
6.5 The Authority reasons market by market and hazardous waste incineration is one
6.6 The Suez precedent sets the rules and leaves an opening
6.7 Other buyers exist and Veolia loses by letting them act.
6.8 Our assumptions give Chauny about €2m of EBITDA and a price of some twenty million
6.9 Calculated as Veolia calculates them, the criteria shift the focus of the test towards ROCE and earnings accretion
6.10 Veolia would bring the incinerator what it lacks to meet the criteria
6.11 Applied to Veolia’s recent acquisitions, the payback period shows that our cap is conservative
6.12 Two further objections: the priority given to the rest of the world and the site’s liabilities
6.13 US platforms remain out of reach or unpriced
6.14 What we could not establish
7. Bid for the Chauny incinerator under a price cap, continue the tuck-ins and wait for disposals before a platform
7.1 We recommend a capped bid for Chauny, named tuck-ins and no platform before new disposals
7.2 Chauny’s value lies in its return, not its size
7.3 The Authority’s decision dictates three courses of action
7.4 Caution is paid for in EBITDA given up and the rating agencies carry the risk
7.5 Veolia has confirmed GreenUp, and our model projects 2027 EBITDA just below the target
7.6 Four observable thresholds would cause us to change our view
7.7 What we could not establish
Conclusion
The remaining capacity funds tuck-ins, and the first one has a name
Leverage, not the GreenUp envelope, limits Veolia's acquisitions
A capped bid for Chauny, tuck-ins and no transaction on the scale of Clean Earth
A figure is read on its page, headroom is read in probabilities
